prompt: Some people think students should be allowed to use calculators in all math classes. Write an essay arguing for or against this.
text:
# Calculators Belong in Math Class, but Not in Every Math Class

Calculators are useful, and no one should ban them. But the claim that students should be allowed to use them in all math classes goes too far. Some classes exist to teach skills a calculator would do for the student, and in those classes the tool defeats the purpose.

Start with what a calculator does well. It handles tedious arithmetic quickly and without errors. In a physics problem, a statistics project or a unit on compound interest, the goal is to understand the model, not to multiply seven-digit numbers by hand. A student who spends twenty minutes on long division has less time to think about what the answer means. In these settings, calculators let students work on harder and more interesting problems.

The trouble is that early math classes have a different goal. A third grader learning that 7 × 8 is 56 is not just collecting an answer. She is building number sense, a feel for how quantities relate. That feel is what lets an older student notice that 48 × 52 can't be 25,000, or that a bank statement looks wrong. Students who always reach for a calculator never build it. They also can't catch their own mistakes, such as a mistyped digit or a missing parenthesis, because they have no sense of what a reasonable answer looks like.

Fluency with basic facts also frees up working memory. When a student has to stop and work out 6 × 7 in the middle of a fraction problem, she loses track of the larger task. Students who know their facts by heart can focus on the new idea. A calculator can't give them that. It only helps once they have already learned to do without it.

Algebra shows a similar problem. A student who types an equation into a graphing calculator and reads off the solution has not learned why the solution works. Factoring, simplifying and rearranging are the skills the class is meant to teach, and they are also the habits of reasoning that later courses depend on. If the calculator does that work, the student gets the right answer and learns very little.

Supporters of unlimited use often say that calculators are everywhere, so schools should prepare students for the world they will live in. This is a fair point, but it proves less than it seems to. Adults also carry phones with maps, yet we still teach children to read a street sign. The question is not whether a tool will exist later. It is whether a student can understand and check the tool's output. People who know the underlying math can use a calculator well, and people who don't can only trust it.

A better policy is to match the tool to the lesson. Early grades should focus on mental math and paper methods. Middle school can bring in calculators for checking work and for problems where the arithmetic is not the point. In high school and college, calculators should be standard for statistics, calculus applications and science courses, and teachers can still design some tests without them to confirm that students understand the methods.

This approach asks teachers to decide, class by class and unit by unit, what each lesson is for. That is harder than a single rule, but it is the only approach that serves both goals: students who can do the work, and students who understand it.

So calculators should be welcome in most math classes, but not all. A blanket rule would trade the foundation of mathematical understanding for convenience, and students would pay for it in every later course.
